title: Ring of Fire
keyIdea: Earthquakes and volcanoes do not happen just anywhere. Most of them happen in long lines, and the biggest line is a horseshoe round the edge of the Pacific Ocean called the Ring of Fire. It runs from New Zealand, up past Indonesia and Japan, across to Alaska and down the west coast of the Americas to Chile. These lines are where the giant plates that make up Earth's rocky outside meet and move.
familyTip: Look at a world map or globe together and find the Pacific Ocean. Trace round its edge with a finger: New Zealand, Indonesia, the Philippines, Japan, Alaska, California, Mexico, Peru and Chile. Then look up the news for the last big earthquake and see if it was on your ring.

visual.caption: Is each place on the Ring of Fire, round the Pacific edge, or not? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: drop earthquakes and volcanoes on a map, trace the Ring of Fire, find the plate edges, then check which places are on it.

kid: Earthquakes and volcanoes do not pop up just anywhere. If you mark every big earthquake on a map, the marks make lines. Volcanoes sit in the same lines.

The biggest line goes round the edge of the Pacific Ocean, like a giant horseshoe. It is called the Ring of Fire. It runs from New Zealand up past Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan, across to Alaska, and down the coast of the Americas to Chile.

Why there? Earth's rocky outside is cut into huge pieces called plates. They move very slowly, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Where two plates push, pull or slide past each other, the ground can shake. Rock can melt and come up as a volcano.

The Ring of Fire is not real fire. It is a name for all those volcanoes and earthquakes. Places in the middle of a plate, like the middle of Australia or Brazil, are far from an edge. Big earthquakes are rare there, and they have no active volcanoes.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This matches NGSS 4-ESS2-2: analyse and interpret data from maps to describe patterns of Earth's features, including the locations of earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain ranges. In England it fits key stage 2 geography: describe and understand physical geography, including volcanoes and earthquakes. Key words: earthquake, volcano, pattern, Ring of Fire, plate, plate boundary or edge, Pacific Ocean, map.

The US Geological Survey says that about 81% of the world's largest earthquakes happen along the Ring of Fire. It is about 40,000 km long and has about 450 volcanoes, roughly three quarters of the world's active volcanoes. Most of the rest are in the Alpide belt, from the Mediterranean through Iran to the Himalaya, and along mid-ocean ridges. The lab map is a simple picture, not to scale, and its dots are drawn to match these real patterns.

Common mistakes: thinking earthquakes and volcanoes are random or spread evenly; thinking they happen in hot places, so the Sun or a hot climate causes them; thinking cities or people cause big earthquakes; taking the name literally, as a ring of real fire on the sea; and thinking the middle of a big country is just as likely to have a big quake.

In the lab your child drops 90 earthquakes and sees them fall in lines. They add volcanoes in the same lines and trace the ring with a finger. Then they tap quakes to see which two plates meet there, and check eight places to find the five that are on the ring.

practice.prompt: Where do most big earthquakes happen?
choices: In lines round the edge of the Pacific Ocean
In the middle of big countries
practice.hint: Think of the map with all the red dots.
practice.explain: Most big earthquakes line up round the Pacific Ocean, in the Ring of Fire.

practice.prompt: A map shows {n} groups of 10 big earthquakes. In each group of 10, about 8 are on the Ring of Fire. How many are on the ring?
practice.hint: Each group gives 8 quakes on the ring. Count in 8s, or multiply.
practice.explain: {n} × 8 = {=8*n}, so about {=8*n} of the {=10*n} quakes are on the ring.

practice.prompt: Why do earthquakes happen in lines?
choices: They happen where Earth's plates meet
Hot weather makes the ground crack
practice.hint: What did the dashed lines on the map show?
practice.explain: Earth's rocky outside is cut into plates. Earthquakes happen where plates meet and move.

practice.prompt: Volcanoes are found in {a} places on one part of the ring and {b} on another. How many is that in all?
Which place is on the Ring of Fire?
practice.hint: Look for a place on the edge of the Pacific Ocean.
practice.explain: Chile is on the Pacific coast of South America, where two plates meet. Brazil and the middle of Australia are far from a plate edge.

pool.prompt: What is the Ring of Fire?
choices: A horseshoe of volcanoes and earthquakes round the Pacific
A ring of real fire on the sea
pool.hint: It is a name for a pattern on the map.
pool.explain: The Ring of Fire is the long line of volcanoes and earthquakes round the edge of the Pacific Ocean.

pool.prompt: Which ocean does the Ring of Fire go round?
pool.hint: It is the biggest ocean, in the middle of the lab map.
pool.explain: The ring goes round the edge of the Pacific, the biggest ocean.

pool.prompt: A plate creeps about 5 cm each year. How far does it move in {y} years (cm)?
pool.hint: Each year adds 5 cm. Count in 5s, or multiply.
pool.explain: {y} × 5 = {=5*y} cm. Plates are slow: that is about the length of a hand for every few years.

pool.prompt: Some volcanoes are split into {g} groups of 4. In each group, 3 are on the ring. How many volcanoes are on the ring?
pool.hint: Each group of 4 gives 3 on the ring. Count in 3s, or multiply.
pool.explain: {g} × 3 = {=3*g}, so {=3*g} of the {=4*g} volcanoes are on the ring.

pool.prompt: Earth's rocky outside is cut into huge pieces. What are they called?
pool.hint: The dashed lines on the map were their edges.
pool.explain: The pieces are called plates. They move slowly, and earthquakes happen at their edges.

pool.prompt: Which place is not on the Ring of Fire?
pool.hint: Which one is far from the Pacific edge?
pool.explain: Brazil is in the middle of a plate, far from the Pacific edge. Japan and New Zealand are on the ring.

pool.prompt: Alaska is cold. Is it on the Ring of Fire?
choices: Yes, it is at a plate edge by the Pacific
No, it is too far north
pool.hint: Does heat from the Sun make earthquakes?
pool.explain: Alaska is on the ring. Earthquakes come from plates moving, not from hot weather.

pool.prompt: Ella says earthquakes can happen anywhere just as often. What is right?
choices: Most happen in lines at plate edges
pool.hint: Remember the map: were the dots spread out evenly?
pool.explain: The map shows lines, not an even spread. Most quakes are at plate edges.

pool.prompt: How fast do Earth's plates move?
choices: Very slowly, about as fast as fingernails grow
pool.hint: You cannot feel them moving day to day.
pool.explain: Plates move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow.
